chapter_theme: The body of a realized jnani must not be burned or left to animals: that is like setting fire to the Lord's temple and brings drought, famine and the fall of kings. It is to be buried seated in a cave-tomb, and the chapter prescribes the tomb's measures, sites, furnishings, offerings and the shrine set over it, which brings grace to the land.
structure_note: Three warnings against burning or exposure (1910 to 1912) and one promise for burial (1913) are followed by a manual of the rite: measures (1914, 1916), sites (1915), lining and seat (1917, 1918), placing the body (1919), offerings and closing (1920, 1921), and the linga or tree set on top with the sixteen services (1922).

1910.reading: If the body of a boundless jnani is burned, the whole land burns with fever; if dogs and jackals feed on it, strife comes and the world itself becomes food for dogs and jackals.
1910.nuance: The punishment mirrors the wrong: fire for fire, dogs and jackals for dogs and jackals. நுண்செரு, read here as strife, is an unusual word.

1911.reading: If fire touches the body of a jnani beyond reckoning, it is as if the Lord's own temple were set alight; rain fails, the world falls into famine and countless kings lose their kingdoms.
1911.nuance: அண்ணல்தம் கோயில் makes the jnani's body the Lord's temple, a claim Tirumular makes of the body generally elsewhere. The harm is to the whole land and its rulers, not only to those who burn the body.

1912.reading: Burying such people is an act of merit; heaping fire on them brings ruin to the land, letting the body decay in the open disgraces it, and the whole world is thrown into confusion by the spreading fire.
1912.nuance: The third line, மண்ணில் அழியில் அலங்கார பங்கமாம், is taken as decay on open ground spoiling the body's dignity, but it could also mean harm to the land's order. The verse names burial as புண்ணியம், merit, and not just as the lesser evil.

1913.reading: When the boundless jnani has reached grace, if that body is kept in a cave-tomb, fine kings and all who live on the ancient earth receive grace and joy without end.
1913.nuance: This is the reverse of 1910 to 1912: where burning harms land and kings, the kept body blesses them. குகை, cave, is the chapter's word for the tomb.

1914.reading: The pit is dug a good nine spans deep, its surround measured at five spans, the inner cave made triangular at three spans; in this birth-ending cave the body sits in the lotus posture.
1914.nuance: The measures nine, five and three are clear, but what குவைமிகு சூழ (the surround) refers to is not. பவமறு (ending birth) gives the tomb a part in the jnani's release, or marks it as fit for one already released.

1915.reading: One's own house, a hall, a tank bank, the land between rivers, a flower grove, good ground in a town, a forest beyond thought and a high mountain slope are the places fit for the cave-tomb.
1915.nuance: The list runs from the household to the wilderness, so the tomb is not confined to remote or sacred ground.

1916.reading: The verse gives further proportions for the cave: a fourfold enclosure, a base of five parts and of nine set true, and an arrangement three by three, done exactly by those who perform the rite.
1916.nuance: பஞ்சாங்க பாதம், நவபாதம் and பொற்பமா ஓசமும் are obscure, and the arithmetic cannot be fixed from the Tamil. Only the stress on exact measure is clear.

1917.reading: Five metals and nine gems are spread out abundantly, a seat placed over them, munja grass laid on it and white ash on that, and a pouch of fine gold powder may also be set there.
1917.nuance: பஞ்ச லோகம் and நவமணி are the standard five metals and nine gems of temple consecration, which treats the tomb like a shrine.

1918.reading: With the fourfold enclosure laid in the cave, put on it a garland dripping honey, sandal paste, musk, clear sandal, civet and rose water, and offer bright incense gladly.

1919.reading: The body is dusted with sacred ash and clothed, set on the seat, adorned with fragrant powder, seated on top, and then things are spread over it.
1919.nuance: போதறு கண்ணமும் is unclear: perhaps powder free of buds, or a corrupt form of சுண்ணம். What is spread in the last line, flowers or cloth, is not said.

1920.reading: After spreading, the four sides are filled in, fried vegetables, cooked rice and tender coconut set down, and after a further act the cover above is closed.
1920.nuance: குருத்தலம் வைத்துஓர் குழைமுகம் பார்வை தரித்தபின் is obscure: it may refer to a guru's place, a face with ear-rings or a ritual gaze. The food offerings echo those made to a deity.

1921.reading: White ash, powder, many flowers, darbha grass and bilva are strewn over it, it is bathed with water of the feet, and the ground above is laid out three by three.
1921.nuance: பாத உதகம் is usually water that has washed a holy person's or deity's feet; whose feet is not said. The three-by-three ground repeats 1916.

1922.reading: On the platform above, install one of two, a peepal tree or a Siva linga, with the shrine facing north or east, and perform with love the sixteen services.
1922.nuance: அரசு here is the peepal tree, not kingship. சோடச உபசாரம் is the standard sixteenfold worship of a deity, so the tomb becomes a temple.

links.note: Both speak of what is done with a corpse once its life has left. The Naladiyar asks what it matters whether it is dragged off, buried or thrown anywhere; Tirumular says that burning or exposing a jnani's body ruins the land. The conflict holds if the Naladiyar's indifference covers every body; if it speaks only of ordinary people, Tirumular's exception for the jnani escapes it.

Both tie the failure of rain to a wrong: in the Kural a king's crooked rule, in Tirumular the burning of a jnani's body. The same belief that the sky answers moral or sacred offence is applied to kingship and to the rites of the dead.
1823 makes the body of flesh a temple of the Lord; 1911 draws the consequence for the jnani's corpse: to burn it is to set fire to the Lord's temple.

1868 says that where one seeker of the Lord lives 'பார்மழை பெய்யும்', rain falls and the land has no want. 1911 gives the reverse: if fire touches the jnani's body 'மண்ணில் மழைவிழா', rain fails, famine comes and kings lose their kingdoms. Together they make the holy one's presence, living and dead, the condition of rain and of the land's welfare.

1912 says burying the jnani 'புண்ணியமாம்', is merit, while heaping fire on him ruins the land and letting him decay in the open disgraces him. Naladiyar 26 says that once the dancer has left the skin bag it does not matter whether the body is dragged off, 'நன்றாய்ந்து அடக்கிலென்', carefully buried, or thrown away. One makes the disposal of the body decisive and the other declares it meaningless.

1882 says the land where a 'சிவயோகி ஞானி' dwells gains knowers and good order and becomes the higher world. 1913 says that if the jnani's body is kept in a cave-tomb, kings and all who live on the earth 'அந்தமில் இன்ப அருள்பெறுவாரே'. 1913 extends 1882's blessing of place from the living sage to his tomb.

1911 says fire touching the jnani's body is 'அண்ணல்தம் கோயில் அழல்இட்டது', like setting the Lord's own temple ablaze. 1922 ends the burial rite by installing a Siva linga over the tomb and performing 'சோடசம் ... உபசாரம்', the sixteen services of temple worship. The rite makes literal what 1911 put as a simile: the jnani's body is a temple.

source_issues: 1916 line 3 (பொற்பமா ஓசமும்) and 1920 line 3 (குருத்தலம் வைத்துஓர் குழைமுகம் பார்வை) are obscure and may be corrupt.
1919 line 3: போதறு கண்ணமும் may be a corruption of சுண்ணம் (powder), which appears in 1917.
